title: Concrete technology
summary: The water–cement ratio governs everything — strength, permeability and durability — and Abrams' law is the single most useful idea in the subchapter. Learn the mix design target f'_ck = f_ck + 1.65σ, because a mix designed at exactly f_ck fails acceptance about half the time. The durability tables (w/c and cover by exposure) are examined directly, and the defects section pays well: each defect maps to a specific cause, so a question naming a symptom is asking for that cause.

sections.heading: Ingredients and the water–cement ratio
sections.body:
Concrete is **cement + fine aggregate + coarse aggregate + water + admixtures**, with aggregate occupying **60–75%** of the volume and therefore dominating the cost and the volume stability.

**Abrams' law** is the central principle:

> **For a fully compacted concrete of given materials, strength depends chiefly on the WATER–CEMENT RATIO.**

Not on the cement content alone. A rich mix with too much water is weaker than a leaner mix with less — which is why adding cement to compensate for a wet mix does not work, and why the first question about any strength failure is what the w/c ratio actually was.

**The two competing requirements:**

| Lower w/c | Higher w/c |
|---|---|
| **Higher strength** | Lower strength |
| **Lower permeability**, better durability | More permeable |
| Less shrinkage | More shrinkage |
| **Poorer workability** — harder to place and compact | Easier to place |

The resolution is **superplasticisers**, which give workability at a low w/c and so break the trade-off — the basis of all high-strength and self-compacting concrete.

**Limits worth knowing:**

| w/c | Significance |
|---|---|
| **≈ 0.25** | Below this, **hydration is incomplete** — there is not enough water to hydrate the cement |
| **≈ 0.38** | The theoretical minimum for **complete hydration** with no capillary porosity |
| 0.40 – 0.45 | Durable structural concrete |
| **0.50 – 0.55** | Ordinary concrete; the code maximum for mild and moderate exposure |
| Above 0.6 | Weak and permeable; not permitted in RCC |

**Maximum w/c by exposure (IS 456 Table 5)** — a durability requirement, not a strength one:

| Exposure | Max w/c | Min grade | Min cement (kg/m³) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mild** | **0.55** | **M20** | 300 |
| **Moderate** | **0.50** | **M25** | 300 |
| **Severe** | **0.45** | **M30** | 320 |
| **Very severe** | **0.45** | **M35** | 340 |
| **Extreme** | **0.40** | **M40** | 360 |

Note that **M20 is the minimum grade for reinforced concrete** in any exposure, and that the table specifies a **minimum cement content** as well as a maximum w/c — because a very lean mix, however low its w/c, lacks the paste to fill the aggregate voids and seal the concrete.

**Aggregate requirements** (IS 383): clean, strong, durable, chemically inert, of suitable **grading** and **shape**, free of deleterious material. **Fine aggregate passes the 4.75 mm sieve**; coarse is retained on it. Grading zones **I (coarsest) to IV (finest)**, with **Zone II the reference** for mix design.

**Water** must be free of oils, acids, alkalis, salts, sugar and organic matter. **Seawater must not be used in RCC** because its chlorides corrode the reinforcement — though it may be used in plain concrete where no steel is present. The practical test: water fit to drink is generally fit for concrete, but the converse does not hold.

**Admixtures (IS 9103):**

| Type | Effect | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Plasticiser** | Workability at the same w/c, or 5–15% less water | — |
| **Superplasticiser** | **15–30% water reduction** | The basis of high-strength and self-compacting concrete |
| **Accelerator** | Faster set and early strength | **Calcium chloride is banned in RCC** — it corrodes steel |
| **Retarder** | Delays setting | Hot weather, long hauls, large pours |
| **Air-entraining** | 3–6% microscopic bubbles | Greatly improves **freeze–thaw** resistance; costs ~5% strength per 1% air |
| Waterproofing | Reduces permeability | — |
| **Mineral admixtures** — fly ash, silica fume, GGBS | Pozzolanic; denser, less permeable, lower heat | Slower early strength, so **longer curing** |

**Silica fume** deserves note: its particles are about a hundred times finer than cement, so it fills the space between cement grains and reacts with the calcium hydroxide that hydration liberates. The result is a much denser paste — which is why it is used for high-strength and high-durability concrete despite its cost.

sections.heading: Mix design
sections.body:
**Nominal mixes** (IS 456 Table 9) are prescriptive volume proportions, permitted only up to **M20** and only for small works:

| Grade | Nominal proportion |
|---|---|
| M5 | 1 : 5 : 10 |
| M10 | 1 : 3 : 6 |
| M15 | 1 : 2 : 4 |
| **M20** | **1 : 1.5 : 3** |
| M25 | 1 : 1 : 2 (by tradition; design mix required) |

Beyond M20 a **design mix** is mandatory, because nominal proportions take no account of the actual aggregate grading, shape, moisture or cement strength — so they are necessarily conservative and wasteful, and above M20 they cannot reliably reach the strength at all.

**The design target — the most examined item in the subchapter:**

> **f′_ck = f_ck + 1.65 σ**

The **1.65** is the standard normal deviate for the **5% fractile** that defines characteristic strength. Assumed standard deviations from **IS 10262:2019**:

| Grade | σ (N/mm²) |
|---|---|
| M10 – M15 | 3.5 |
| **M20 – M25** | **4.0** |
| **M30 – M45** | **5.0** |
| M50 and above | 6.0 |

**A worked case for M25:** target = 25 + 1.65 × 4.0 = **31.6 N/mm²**. The mix must be designed for about 31.6, **not 25** — and a mix designed at exactly 25 will fail the acceptance criteria roughly half the time, since by definition half the results fall below the mean.

**The consequence of good quality control** follows directly: a contractor with a smaller σ needs a **lower target mean**, hence **less cement** for the same characteristic strength. Quality control pays for itself in material saved, not merely in fewer rejections.

**The IS 10262 procedure**, in outline:

1. Target strength from f_ck and σ.
2. **Water–cement ratio** from the target strength, capped by the **durability** limit for the exposure — whichever is lower governs.
3. **Water content** from the maximum aggregate size and required workability, adjusted for admixtures.
4. **Cement content** = water ÷ (w/c), checked against the durability **minimum**.
5. **Coarse aggregate volume** from the maximum size and the fine aggregate zone, corrected if the sand is not Zone II.
6. Fine aggregate by **absolute volume**.
7. **Trial mixes**, adjustment, and confirmation by cube tests.

Step 2 is where candidates go wrong: **the durability requirement often governs over the strength requirement**, particularly for lower grades in severe exposure. A mix satisfying M25's strength at w/c = 0.55 is not acceptable in severe exposure, where 0.45 is the maximum.

**Acceptance criteria (IS 456 cl. 16).** For concrete of grade M15 and above, both must hold:

> The **mean of any four consecutive** samples ≥ f_ck + 0.825σ (or f_ck + 3, whichever is greater)
> **Each individual** sample ≥ f_ck − 3 N/mm²

So one low cube does **not** automatically mean rejection — it triggers investigation. If the concrete fails, the options in order are: **check by core tests or non-destructive testing**, **load testing** of the member, **strengthening**, or **rejection and removal**.

**Maximum aggregate size** is limited by the least of: **¼ of the minimum section dimension**, **5 mm less than the clear spacing between bars**, and **5 mm less than the clear cover**. Typically **20 mm** for ordinary work, **10 or 12 mm** for thin or heavily reinforced sections, and up to **40 mm** for mass concrete — a larger size reduces water demand and hence cement, which is why mass concrete uses the largest practicable aggregate.

sections.heading: Fresh concrete — workability, production and placing
sections.body:
**Workability** is the ease with which concrete can be **mixed, transported, placed, compacted and finished without segregation**. It is not a single physical property, which is why several tests exist and each suits a different consistency:

| Test | Suits | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| **Slump** (cone 200/100/300 mm, 4 layers × 25 strokes) | **Medium** — the site standard | IS 1199 |
| **Compaction factor** | **Low** workability, dry mixes | IS 1199 |
| **Vee-Bee consistometer** | **Very dry** mixes | IS 1199 |
| Flow table | Very wet, flowing mixes | — |

Typical slumps: **20–50 mm** road pavements and mass concrete, **50–100 mm** ordinary RCC, **100–150 mm** congested sections, **150–200 mm** tremie or pumped concrete.

The **shape of the slump** is diagnostic: a **true** slump indicates a cohesive mix, a **shear** slump a harsh non-cohesive one liable to segregate, and a **collapse** slump one far too wet.

**Factors affecting workability:** water content (dominant), **aggregate shape** (rounded better than angular), **grading** (well-graded better), maximum size, **fines content**, cement content, admixtures, and time and temperature since mixing.

**Batching.** **By weight is far more accurate than by volume**, and the reason is **bulking of sand**: moist sand occupies up to **20–40% more volume** at about 4–6% moisture, because surface moisture films push the grains apart. Volume batching therefore silently **under-supplies sand**, giving a harsh, under-sanded mix. Where volume batching is unavoidable, the bulking must be measured and the volume corrected.

**Mixing** should continue at least **2 minutes** in a machine mixer (**1½–2 minutes** typical), with the order of charging arranged so the cement is not left dry against the drum. **Hand mixing** is permitted only for small unimportant work, with **10% extra cement** to compensate for its inferior uniformity.

**Transport and placing.** The requirements are to avoid **segregation** and to place before the concrete stiffens. **Free fall should not exceed about 1.5 m**; a chute or tremie is used for greater drops. Layers should be **300–450 mm** thick, each compacted before the next, and placing should be **continuous** between construction joints — a **cold joint** forms if the previous layer has set, and it is a plane of weakness and permeability.

**Compaction** expels **entrapped air**, and its importance is easily underestimated: **5% voids can reduce strength by about 30%**. Methods: hand rodding (only for thin sections), **internal (needle) vibrator** (the standard for beams and columns), **surface (screed) vibrator** (slabs and pavements), **form vibrator** (thin walls and precast), and **table vibrator** (precast units).

**Over-vibration causes segregation** — the coarse aggregate settles and a laitance of paste rises — so vibration must stop when air bubbles cease to appear and the surface glistens. Under-vibration leaves **honeycombing**, over-vibration leaves a weak surface layer; both are workmanship defects invisible on a drawing.

**Curing** maintains satisfactory moisture and temperature so **hydration continues**:

| Cement | Minimum curing |
|---|---|
| **OPC** | **7 days** |
| **PPC, blended cements, mineral admixtures** | **10 – 14 days** |
| Hot or dry weather | Extended |

Methods: **ponding**, wet coverings (hessian, sand), **continuous sprinkling**, membrane curing compounds, and **steam curing** for precast.

**Stopping curing early can cost 30–40% of the potential strength** and greatly increases permeability, because the surface zone — which is the very layer protecting the reinforcement — is the part that dries first. Concrete gains about **65–70% of its 28-day strength by 7 days**, and continues gaining slowly for years while moisture remains available.

sections.heading: Properties of hardened concrete and its defects
sections.body:
**Strength relations:**

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Characteristic compressive strength** | f_ck, on a **150 mm cube** at 28 days |
| **Modulus of elasticity** | **E_c = 5000 √f_ck** N/mm² |
| **Flexural strength (modulus of rupture)** | **f_cr = 0.7 √f_ck** N/mm² |
| Split tensile strength | ≈ 0.9 f_cr |
| **Direct tensile strength** | **≈ 1/10** of the compressive |
| Cylinder strength | ≈ 0.8 × cube |

Note that both **E_c and f_cr vary as √f_ck**, so doubling the grade does **not** double the stiffness or the tensile strength — it increases them by only about 40%. That is why higher grades are used for **strength and durability**, not for stiffness, and why deflection is rarely solved by increasing the grade.

**Creep and shrinkage** — the distinction is examined directly:

| | **Creep** | **Shrinkage** |
|---|---|---|
| Requires load? | **Yes** — sustained load | **No** — occurs unloaded |
| Cause | Time-dependent deformation of the paste under stress | Loss of moisture (drying) and chemical (autogenous) change |
| IS 456 value | **Creep coefficient 2.2 at 7 days, 1.6 at 28 days, 1.1 at 1 year** of loading age | **Ultimate shrinkage strain 0.0003** |

Both matter because together they make the **long-term deflection two to three times** the immediate value — which is why IS 456's span/depth ratios are as conservative as they are, and why **compression steel** is provided partly to restrain creep.

**Durability** is a function of **permeability** above all, since every deterioration mechanism requires the ingress of water or ions. The controls are therefore: **low w/c**, **adequate cement content**, **full compaction**, **proper curing**, and **adequate cover**.

**Nominal cover (IS 456 Table 16):**

| Exposure | Cover |
|---|---|
| **Mild** | **20 mm** |
| **Moderate** | **30 mm** |
| **Severe** | **45 mm** |
| **Very severe** | **50 mm** |
| **Extreme** | **75 mm** |
| **Footings** | **50 mm** minimum |

Cover must also be **at least the bar diameter**, and it protects against both **corrosion** and **fire**. Inadequate cover is the **single commonest cause of premature failure** in reinforced concrete, and it is a workmanship failure — the drawing usually specifies it correctly and the cover blocks are then omitted or crushed underfoot.

**Deterioration mechanisms:**

| Mechanism | Process | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **Corrosion of reinforcement** | Carbonation or chloride ingress destroys the passive film; rust **expands ~6 times**, spalling the cover | **Cover**, low permeability, chloride limits |
| **Sulphate attack** | Sulphates react with C₃A forming expansive ettringite | **Sulphate resisting cement**, low C₃A, low permeability |
| **Chloride attack** | Depassivates steel | Limit chloride content; never use seawater in RCC |
| **Alkali–aggregate reaction** | Reactive silica + alkalis form an expansive gel | Non-reactive aggregate, low-alkali cement, pozzolans |
| **Freeze–thaw** | Water expands 9% on freezing | **Air entrainment**, low permeability |
| **Abrasion and erosion** | Mechanical wear | Hard aggregate, high strength, good curing |

The **corrosion mechanism is self-accelerating**, which is why it dominates: rust occupies several times the volume of the steel it came from, so it cracks and spalls the cover, admitting more water and chloride to a larger area of steel.

**Defects and their causes** — each symptom maps to a specific cause, and a question naming the symptom is asking for it:

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Segregation** | Over-wet or harsh mix, **over-vibration**, dropping from a height |
| **Bleeding** | Excess water rising, leaving a weak porous **laitance** |
| **Honeycombing** | **Inadequate compaction**, congested reinforcement, leaking formwork |
| **Cold joint** | Delay in placing the next layer |
| **Plastic shrinkage cracking** | Rapid surface drying **before** setting — hot, dry, windy conditions |
| **Drying shrinkage cracking** | Restrained shrinkage after hardening |
| **Crazing** | Rich or over-trowelled surface |
| **Efflorescence** | Salts carried to the surface by moisture |
| **Laitance** | Weak paste layer from bleeding — must be **removed** before the next lift |
| **Spalling** | Corrosion of reinforcement, or fire |

**Plastic shrinkage cracking** is worth distinguishing from drying shrinkage: it occurs **within hours, before the concrete has set**, when surface evaporation exceeds the rate at which bleed water rises. The remedy is not more curing water afterwards but **preventing the evaporation** — windbreaks, fog spraying, evaporation retarders, and placing at cooler times of day.

**Special concretes**, examined by name:

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **High strength** | M60 and above; low w/c, superplasticiser, **silica fume** |
| **High performance** | Specified for durability as well as strength |
| **Self-compacting** | Flows and compacts under its own weight; congested sections |
| **Fibre reinforced** | Steel, glass or polypropylene fibres; **controls cracking**, improves toughness |
| **Lightweight** | Lightweight aggregate or aerated; insulation, reduced dead load |
| **Pumpable** | Well graded, adequate fines, higher slump |
| **Shotcrete / guniting** | Sprayed; **tunnel lining**, slope stabilisation, repair |
| **Ferrocement** | Thin sections with wire mesh; water tanks, boats |
| **Ready mixed** | Batched at a plant; better control, but **transport time** limits apply |
| **Roller compacted** | Very dry, compacted by roller; dams and pavements |

**Shotcrete matters in Nepal** for tunnel support and slope stabilisation, and **ferrocement** for the small water tanks used in rural water supply — both being techniques that need little plant and can be executed remotely.

formulas.label: Target mean strength for mix design
formulas.note: σ = 4.0 for M20–M25, 5.0 for M30–M45. M25 needs a target of about 31.6 N/mm², not 25.

formulas.label: Modulus of elasticity and flexural strength
formulas.note: Both vary as √f_ck, so doubling the grade raises them only about 40%.

formulas.label: Durability limits (IS 456 Table 5)
formulas.expression: mild 0.55/M20 ; moderate 0.50/M25 ; severe 0.45/M30 ; very severe 0.45/M35 ; extreme 0.40/M40
formulas.note: Durability often governs over strength. M20 is the minimum grade for RCC in any exposure.

formulas.label: Nominal cover (IS 456 Table 16)
formulas.expression: mild 20 ; moderate 30 ; severe 45 ; very severe 50 ; extreme 75 mm ; footings 50 mm
formulas.note: Also at least the bar diameter. Inadequate cover is the commonest cause of premature RCC failure.

formulas.label: Acceptance criteria (IS 456 cl. 16)
formulas.expression: mean of any 4 consecutive ≥ f_ck + 0.825σ (or f_ck + 3);  each individual ≥ f_ck − 3
formulas.note: One low cube triggers investigation, not automatic rejection.

formulas.label: Maximum aggregate size
formulas.expression: least of ¼ minimum section dimension, (clear bar spacing − 5 mm), (cover − 5 mm)
formulas.note: Typically 20 mm; up to 40 mm in mass concrete, where a larger size reduces water and cement demand.

formulas.label: Creep and shrinkage (IS 456)
formulas.expression: creep coefficient 2.2 (7 d), 1.6 (28 d), 1.1 (1 yr) ;   ultimate shrinkage strain 0.0003
formulas.note: Together they make long-term deflection 2–3 times the immediate value.

formulas.label: Bulking of sand
formulas.expression: Bulking % = (V_moist − V_dry)/V_dry × 100 — peaks at 20–40% around 4–6% moisture
formulas.note: Why volume batching under-supplies sand. Batch by MASS.
